objective.statement: Move session storage from in-memory to Redis so the API can run with two replicas.
objective.success_definition: Session storage is backed by Redis, the API can run with two replicas, sessions survive a rolling restart, the AuthProvider interface is unchanged, and existing tests pass.

goals.statement: Move session storage from in-memory storage to Redis.
acceptance: Session data is stored in and served from Redis rather than in-memory structures

goals.statement: Enable the API to run with two replicas.
acceptance: The API can run with two replicas

goals.statement: Ensure sessions survive a rolling restart.

assumptions.statement: A Redis instance will be available for the API to connect to in the target deployment.
Session storage changes are confined to the session storage module of the API codebase.
A Redis client library may be added as a dependency.

open_questions.question: Must existing in-memory sessions be migrated to Redis, or may they be dropped during the cutover?
What session expiration/TTL semantics, if any, should apply to sessions stored in Redis?
options: Preserve current in-memory session expiration behavior

verification.spec: Run the existing test suite against the Redis-backed session storage implementation.
Run the API with two replicas backed by Redis, establish a session on one replica, restart replicas in a rolling fashion, and confirm the session remains valid.
verification.expected: Session survives the rolling restart while two replicas are running

deliverables.description: Redis-backed session storage implementation replacing the in-memory store.

factors: Session data loss if existing in-memory sessions are not migrated
Redis availability becomes a runtime dependency for session storage
Rolling-restart correctness depends on Redis connection handling across replicas
